paragraphs: Robotics Technicians (O*NET 17-3024.01) install, program, troubleshoot, test, or maintain robots and related automated production line equipment. First see whether an equipment fault can be safely isolated, diagnosed, and retested, then judge whether you are willing to do on-site technical work over the long term.

Share some skills with robotics engineers, electromechanical technicians, and industrial machinery maintenance workers; the core of this occupation is equipment installation, controller and sensor troubleshooting, maintenance records, and authorized functional testing.

AI can help look up manuals, compare alarm records, and draft test steps; actual wiring, equipment status, fault causes, and return-to-service authorization must be verified by authorized personnel according to on-site procedures.

Before starting the job, verify the robot model, controller, end tools, production line interfaces, energy isolation, testing authority, shift arrangements, and training requirements; practice materials must not be connected to real equipment.

U.S. robotics technicians 17-3024.01 have no separate 2025 wages and 2025—2035 employment; O*NET cites a median of 73,900 U.S. dollars for the "Electro-Mechanical and Mechatronics Technologists and Technicians" 17-3024 parent occupation, with BLS parent occupation growth of 2.6% and about 1,400 openings per year. Precise occupation wages for China were not obtained.

O*NET 17-3024.01 defines robotics technicians as building, installing, testing, or maintaining robotic equipment and automated production systems. Typical tasks include replacing faulty sensors, controllers, or servo components, diagnosing circuit and mechanical faults, and installing or programming programmable controllers, robot controllers, and conveying equipment.

Occupational identity and tasks follow O*NET 17-3024.01. The wages and employment listed by O*NET belong to the BLS 17-3024 "Electro-Mechanical and Mechatronics Technologists and Technicians" parent occupation; all values on the page must be labeled as parent-occupation figures and cannot be described as independent statistics for robotics technicians.

values: Practice setup｜All fictional, no connection to real equipment
You are a supervised robotics maintenance trainee. Only examine alarms, configurations, and test evidence; do not connect to real equipment or generate motion commands.
A1｜The requirements document calls for operation in a corridor with people; the risk assessment, permitted speed, and stop conditions are not given.
A2｜The sensor log is labeled with the 2026-09-01 calibration version, while the equipment list states the 2026-09-14 version; the two do not match.
A3｜The control program submission number differs from the test report submission number, and the report only records "normal" with no failure scenarios.
A4｜The demo passed in an empty yard, but the customer requires entering a real space with obstacles and foot traffic.
A5｜Technicians should list faults and shutdown recommendations; return to service, parameter changes, and deployment are approved by the authorized team.
Task one: mark items that cannot be released
List A1 unclear personnel exposure conditions, A2 calibration conflict, A3 version inconsistency, and A4 scenario extrapolation; write the status as "pause scenario expansion".

Make a checklist by problem, source material, version, test conditions, responsible person, evidence pending, and status.
